solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Little creatures like snuggling mum and love to be back in the heart of it all

indicators.note: one piece snuggling another wraps itself round it, so the first piece goes on the outside

parts.note: like in the sense 'as', as in 'do as I do'

indicators.text: in the heart of it all
indicators.note: placed in the heart of something means set in its middle, so these letters sit inside the word for mum

parts.note: MA is an informal word for mother
love is nil in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

indicators.note: back means the letters of the phrase to be run backwards

parts.note: to be is the verb be

explanation.surface: A cosy picture of little animals cuddling up to their mother, lovingly settled in the middle of family life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses 'to be'; 'in the heart of it all' sets love and that reversal inside mum, and 'snuggling' wraps 'like' round the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: These single-celled organisms are tiny living creatures, visible only under a microscope.

clue.text: Can it possibly caper?

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters might be arranged some other way, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a tin is able to dance about.
explanation.definitionFit: A caper is a playful or grotesque prank, and an antic is a silly or absurd bit of behaviour.

clue.text: Blade carried round part of prison is spotted

indicators.note: the oar is carried round the other piece, so it goes on the outside

parts.note: the blade of an oar is the flat end, so blade can stand for the oar itself
a cell is one small room of a prison

explanation.surface: A convict's knife, smuggled around a section of jail, gets noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted' reads as 'noticed' but is the definition in the zoological sense of having spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocelli are eye-like spots on wings or skin, so the adjective describes something marked with such spots.

clue.text: One bite that's nasty, to do with pet hate

indicators.note: a nasty version of the two words is a mangled one, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: RE means concerning or to do with, as in a business letter

explanation.surface: A single unpleasant bite from someone's pet dog is the subject of complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' rearranges 'One bite' and 'that's' is a link. The French phrase literally means 'black beast'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's black beast, in the borrowed French phrase, is the thing they most dislike or dread.

clue.text: One's caught in prison fight and commotion

indicators.note: the single letter is caught in the middle of the other pieces, enclosed by them

parts.note: stir is slang for prison
a bout is a boxing match or fight
A means one, as in 'a pound' for 'one pound'

explanation.surface: An inmate gets caught up in a jail brawl and the uproar that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: The word also means porridge, which in British slang is a prison sentence, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirabout is a bustle or a hurly-burly, as well as a porridge stirred in the pot.

clue.text: Brand of comedy to glorify the unemployed

parts.note: Jo Brand is a well-known British stand-up comedian
to bless God is to praise and glorify him

explanation.surface: A style of humour that celebrates people out of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand' looks like a trademark or style; it is the surname of Jo Brand, a British stand-up comedian, so her first name is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without paid work is out of a job, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Old Henry in Japan heartlessly tells us where to go

indicators.note: in places the old Henry inside the trimmed country name
without its heart the word keeps only its first and last letters

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A long-dead Henry in Japan, rather unkindly, gives us directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tells us' is a link between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an American slang name for the toilet, the place one goes when nature calls.

clue.text: A radical? Some mildly tub-thumping revolutionary

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the hidden letters are read backwards
some of the words means a run of their letters is taken

explanation.surface: A political extremist? Hardly, just a rather gently ranting rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes LYTUB from inside 'mildly tub-thumping' and 'revolutionary' turns it round. The definition is chemistry, not politics.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry a radical is a group of atoms acting as a unit, and this four-carbon group is one.

clue.text: Hand over responsibility for Treebeard's disease?

parts.note: Treebeard is a tree-like giant, one of the Ents, in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings
rust is a fungal disease of plants

explanation.surface: Delegating care of the tree-giant's illness to someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of Treebeard's is possessive and links the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone charge of a task or thing is to commit it to their care.

clue.text: Where repairs were made for one pristine yacht initially in broken pieces?

indicators.note: the pieces are broken open and the other letters put in

parts.note: shards are broken pieces of glass or pottery
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: A smart yacht has been smashed to bits; where did it go for mending?
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word; 'in broken' means the word for pieces is split open to take the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dockyards building and mending boats are where ships went for refitting and repair.

clue.text: Criminal twins and they might be like young adults

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two siblings who are crooks, and they might be young people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' rearranges TWINS and THEY; 'and' and 'might be' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Being around the age of twenty fits people in their early adulthood.

clue.text: The whole orchestra show disapproval and one tenor's retiring

parts.note: tut is the clicking sound of disapproval

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A singer leaves while the entire orchestra frowns at him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' turns I and T round to TI.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian musical term instructs all the players to perform together.

clue.text: Wheels around a supply table with dates on it

indicators.note: the car goes around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car
to lend is to supply for a time

explanation.surface: A trolley wheels round a supply of food on a table of dates and fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart or list showing the days of the year is a table laid out by date.

clue.text: Conservative's forte at end of day is obscure

parts.note: forte in music means played loudly

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: The Tory politician's strength, at the close of the day, is hard to grasp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forte' looks like the noun 'strong point' but is the musical marking.
explanation.definitionFit: Something murky or unclear is obscure, like a cloud-filled sky or a muddy liquid.

clue.text: Retreat for home — supermarket bananas left there

parts.note: Morrisons is a British supermarket chain

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: Somebody's home refuge, the supermarket where the fruit was left.
explanation.walkthrough: MORRISONS is a British supermarket chain. 'bananas' rearranges L and THERE to make HELTER.
explanation.definitionFit: This steel cage from the Second World War was put indoors as a refuge from air raids.

clue.text: Is not a nasty stomach upset above all indicative of genetic changes?

indicators.note: above all places this piece at the top of the column, before the others
upset means turned upside down, so in a down clue the word reads upwards

parts.note: tum is an informal word for stomach

indicators.note: nasty means mangled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A queasy stomach upset may be a sign of altered genes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns TUM to MUT, put 'above all' the rest; 'nasty' rearranges IS NOT A to ATIONS. 'indicative of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Changes in the DNA of a gene, passed to offspring, are what biologists call these.

clue.text: Throws out of court such charming people

indicators.note: this piece is outside the court, so it wraps round it

parts.note: shies means throws, as at a coconut shy
a moot is an old assembly or court, and a mock court in law schools

explanation.surface: Smooth talkers get thrown out of court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Suave, ingratiating people with polished manners are called this, often a little suspiciously.

clue.text: Covers up hours involved in targets

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the targets

parts.note: ends are goals or targets, as in 'ends and means'

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone hides the hours spent pursuing their goals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges the letters of 'hours', and 'in' sets that inside the targets.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap something in a burial cloth or veil is to hide it from view.

clue.text: Controversial bias is seen in students getting first in Oxford perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might form something else, so they are rearranged
the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Partiality shows up among university students, maybe the top ones at Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges SEEN IN, STUDENTS and O (the first letter of Oxford); 'getting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Promoting a particular point of view, especially a disputed one, is partisan slant.

clue.text: Accessory Nike etc developed

indicators.note: developed means worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sportswear brands like Nike come out with a new add-on.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie worn round the collar is an item added to an outfit.

clue.text: A letter I put in post out of love captured Helen's heart? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: captured means taken inside, here one piece holding another
the reverse of what is said: the heart of the name does the capturing, not the other way round
the heart of a word is its middle letters, dropping the first and last
the letter I is put inside the shortened post
out of means a letter is removed from the word post

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone posts a love letter that wins Helen's heart, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: POST 'out of' O is PST; I 'put in' gives PIST. 'heart' of HELEN is ELE, and 'Quite the opposite' means ELE 'captured' PIST.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a formal or biblical word for a letter, like those of St Paul.

clue.text: Lorry driver's lost recipe for Sydney's food

indicators.note: the lorry driver has lost a letter, so it is taken out

parts.note: a trucker drives a truck, or lorry
R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin 'take', seen on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A truck driver has mislaid the instructions for a dish made in Sydney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sydney's' points to Australian slang; Sydney is the city, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang this is the everyday word for food or grub.

clue.text: E.g. fair coming to town for starters

definitions.text: E.g. fair coming to town for starters

parts.note: fair means even, as in a fair or even split

indicators.note: for starters means the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A travelling fair arrives in town, to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, a fair rolling into town, while EVEN (fair) plus T (first of town) builds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair arriving in town is an occasion, a happening people go to.

clue.text: Robber initially breaks in for article of theft of our currency

indicators.note: one letter breaks in and takes the place of another

parts.note: stealing is theft
A is the indefinite article

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A burglar breaks in to steal an object, taking British money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our' marks a British setter: the pound is the UK's currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The pound of the United Kingdom is known formally by this name.

clue.text: Piggy craving good grass

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass of wet ground

explanation.surface: A pig longs for fine grazing.
explanation.definitionFit: A gluttonous, pig-like desire for more than one needs is avarice.

clue.text: Given wages and something to eat

definitions.meaning: paid a fee, as a professional is paid for work
a meal, especially for animals or babies

explanation.definitionFit: Read as fee'd it means paid; as a noun it is fodder or a meal.

clue.text: Unconventional about regulation clothes

indicators.note: the words clothe the answer, wrapping round it as a garment does

explanation.surface: Someone is eccentric in their attitude to uniform dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' looks like a noun about uniform but is a verb: the two words wrap the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This borrowed French word means bizarre or beyond the bounds of convention.

clue.text: Quite disturbed — better after removing coat in customs?

indicators.note: after puts the trimmed word behind the rearranged one
disturbed means thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged
taking off the coat strips the outer letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone quite upset feels better after taking a jacket off at passport control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'customs' looks like the border post but means social conventions. 'disturbed' turns QUITE into ETIQU; 'removing coat' leaves ETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Polite social conventions and rules of behaviour are the accepted customs of society.

clue.text: Adult wearing hot tweeds ________?

indicators.note: the letter is inside the other piece, as a body is inside clothes
hot can mean stolen or tampered with, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A grown-up in warm tweed clothing did something; fill in the blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer completes the sentence: an adult in hot tweeds perspired. 'hot' rearranges TWEEDS and A goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone too warmly dressed would perspire, the obvious end to the sentence.

clue.text: Postpone final after find out tip taken from promoter

indicators.note: after puts the last piece behind the others

parts.note: sus, also spelt suss, is slang for find out or work out

indicators.note: the tip of the word is its first letter, taken out

parts.note: the end is the final part

explanation.surface: A promoter delays the final after discovering a hot tip.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold something over until later is to put it off.
